html:
The Garifuna are an Afro-Indigenous people of the Caribbean coast of Central America, in Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua. The map shows their present homeland in 1492, but the Garifuna formed later, on the island of Saint Vincent.

There, in the 1600s and 1700s, Africans who had escaped slavery or survived shipwrecks mixed with the Kalinago (Island Caribs). The British called them Black Caribs. They kept the Kalinago language, an Arawakan tongue, and defended the island against French and British planters.

After the Second Carib War, Britain deported about five thousand Garifuna in 1797, first to a small island off Saint Vincent, where many died, and then to Roatán off Honduras. From there they spread along the mainland coast, living by fishing and farming cassava. Their language, music and dance were declared a masterpiece of humanity's heritage by UNESCO in 2001. Belize marks their arrival every 19 November as Garifuna Settlement Day. See also the Atlantic slave trade.
